cues.x: Extreme Ownership, by Jocko Willink and Leif Babin.
I want to start you in the worst moment of Jocko Willink's professional life, because the entire book grows out of it, and because what he did next is the thing the whole title is named after.
It is 2006, in Ramadi, Iraq, which at that time was one of the most violent places on earth.
Jocko Willink is a Navy SEAL officer, a lieutenant commander, in charge of a unit called Task Unit Bruiser, made up of two SEAL platoons, Charlie and Delta.
Leif Babin, the co-author, commands Charlie platoon.

They are working alongside a large US Army brigade, and their job is to support a strategy of pushing into the city block by block, building small combat outposts in the most dangerous neighbourhoods, and holding them.
On this particular morning there is a large operation under way, with American soldiers, SEAL elements, and Iraqi soldiers all moving through a dense urban area at first light.
Communications are poor.
Units are shifting positions.
And a report comes over the radio: an American unit is in a firefight with enemy fighters holed up in a building.
Except the fighters in that building are not enemy.

They are one of Jocko's own SEAL elements, along with Iraqi soldiers, who had ended up in a building nobody expected them to be in, and who, being fired on, were returning fire, believing themselves to be under attack by insurgents.
This is what the military calls blue on blue, and it is the thing every commander dreads above everything else.

By the time the truth surfaced, an Iraqi soldier was dead, several people were wounded including one of his own men, and the situation was minutes away from air support flattening the building with everyone in it.
Jocko, acting on a feeling that something was badly wrong with the picture he was being given, went in himself, and it stopped.
Afterwards came the investigation.
A commanding officer, a command master chief, and an investigating officer all flew in.
Jocko had to stand in front of his men and his superiors and explain how the unit he ran had shot at itself.
And he had a list.
He had a genuinely excellent list.
Communications had been terrible.
The Iraqi soldiers had moved without telling anyone.
Units had shifted position outside the plan.
A junior leader had not passed a critical piece of information.
Bad intelligence had put people in the wrong place.
Every single item on the list was true, and each one, on its own, was a legitimate contributing cause.
He stood up in front of the room, and he asked whose fault it was.
Somebody said it was his fault, he had made a mistake with a radio call.
Somebody else took responsibility for a positioning error.
And Jocko told them all, no.
He said there was only one person to blame for this, and it was him.
He was the senior man on the battlefield.
He was responsible for everything that happened out there.
He had not communicated adequately with his own leaders.
He had not confirmed positions.
He had not built in the checks that would have prevented it.
Every one of those true, individual causes existed downstream of decisions and systems that were his to make.
He fully expected to be fired.
He assumed his career was finished.
Instead, two things happened.
The investigating team, having watched a commander take the whole weight of it without deflecting a gram, concluded the investigation quickly and the unit was permitted to continue operating.
And, more importantly, something changed inside his own team.
Rather than the leaders becoming defensive and hiding their errors, they began openly owning their mistakes, because they had watched the boss do it first at maximum cost.
The unit got better.
Task Unit Bruiser went on to become one of the most decorated special operations units of the Iraq war.
That is Extreme Ownership.
The leader owns everything in their world.
Everything.
Not most things.
Not the things within their direct control.
Everything.
And I want to be precise about what that means, because it is routinely misunderstood as a slogan about working hard or accepting blame gracefully.
It is neither.
It is a practical claim about where the leverage sits.
If the problem is your subordinate's fault, you are powerless.
If your team failed because your team is bad, there is nothing you can do except complain about your team.

But if the failure is yours, because you did not train them, or brief them clearly, or check that they understood, or build a system that catches the error, then the fix is in your hands and you can start work on it this afternoon.
Extreme Ownership is not primarily a moral position.
It is the only position from which anything can be changed.
Before I go on, let me set the scene properly, because the setting is doing a lot of the work in this book and it deserves more than a sentence.
Ramadi in 2006 was the capital of Anbar Province, and by most accounts the most dangerous city in Iraq.
Large parts of it were controlled outright by insurgents.
American units were being attacked every time they left their bases, sometimes dozens of times a day, with roadside bombs, snipers, and coordinated ambushes.
The prevailing assessment among analysts at the time was that the province was effectively lost.
The strategy that changed it was run by an Army brigade commander, Colonel Sean MacFarland, and it was called seize, clear, hold and build.

Instead of driving out from a large safe base, conducting a raid, and driving back, which surrendered the ground every night, American and Iraqi forces would push into the worst neighbourhoods and build small combat outposts inside them, and then stay.
Live there.
Hold the ground permanently.
It was slow, it was extremely dangerous, and it worked, because it changed the fundamental question a local family faced from "which side will still be here tomorrow" to "which side is already here".
Task Unit Bruiser's role in that was to protect those pushes.

In practice this meant Willink's SEALs moving into buildings in enemy held territory, often in darkness and often ahead of everybody else, occupying rooftops and upper floors, and holding overwatch positions from which they could see and cover the Army and Marine units coming in behind them to build the outposts.
It meant being surrounded, deliberately and repeatedly, for hours at a time.
Leif Babin describes leading his platoon into positions where every window they were not watching was a place from which they could be killed.
That is the crucible the twelve principles came out of.
And it matters for two reasons.
First, because these are not ideas somebody thought up in a seminar room and then illustrated with war stories.
They are the things that were left standing after everything else had been tested by an enemy.

And second, because a book about leadership written by people who watched friends die under their own command has a seriousness to it that survives translation into a corporate context, even when the specific analogy creaks.
Now, the shape of the book.
Willink and Babin wrote it after leaving the military and starting a leadership consultancy, and every chapter has an identical three part structure that makes it extremely easy to follow.
First, a combat story from Ramadi or from SEAL training.
Second, the principle drawn out of it.
Third, a business case study from a real client, showing the same principle in an office, a factory, or a sales team.
Twelve chapters, three sections.
Let me take you through it.
Section one is called Winning the War Within, and it is about the leader's own head.
You have just had chapter one, Extreme Ownership.
Its business case is the one you have almost certainly witnessed.
A vice president of a manufacturing company has a division that keeps missing its numbers, and he explains, at length and persuasively, exactly whose fault this is.
The subordinate leaders are weak.
The market is difficult.
The other division gets better support.
Everything he says is defensible.
And Babin's question to him is simply, what if it were all your fault?
Not as an accusation.
As a hypothesis.
If you accept it, what would you do differently tomorrow?
And suddenly there is a list of actions where before there was only a list of grievances.
Chapter two is the one people remember longest, and it is called There Are No Bad Teams, Only Bad Leaders.
The story is from SEAL training, from the notorious phase known as Hell Week: five and a half days of continuous physical punishment on almost no sleep.
During it, students are divided into boat crews of about seven men, each carrying an inflatable boat on their heads, and made to race, endlessly, on foot and in the surf.
Winners get a few minutes of rest.
Losers go again.
There were two crews at opposite ends of the scale.
Boat Crew Two won almost every race.
Boat Crew Six lost almost every race, and lost badly.

And the men in Boat Crew Six had a culture that follows automatically from constant losing: they blamed each other, they blamed the instructors, they had stopped believing they could win, and they were performing worse every hour.
An instructor decided to run an experiment.
He swapped the two leaders.
The leader of the winning crew went to the losing crew, and the leader of the losing crew went to the winners.
On the very next race, Boat Crew Six, the same seven exhausted, demoralised men who had lost every race for days, won.
And Boat Crew Two, now under the previously losing leader, did not fall apart.
They came in second, right on the heels of the crew that had just beaten them, because the standards that had been built into them held.
That single experiment carries the argument.
Same men.
Same boats.
Same water.
Same exhaustion.
Change one person, and the outcome inverts.
Willink is careful to draw the right conclusion.
It is not that the losing leader was a bad person, or even incompetent in general.
It was that he had accepted the losing.
He had decided the race was already lost and that the reasonable thing was to conserve energy and complain about the unfairness.
The new leader arrived and simply refused to accept it, and the standard he held became the standard the crew met.
Which gives one of the two lines from this book that I would tattoo on a manager's wall: it is not what you preach, it is what you tolerate.
Whatever substandard performance a leader walks past without comment becomes, automatically, the new standard.
Not the thing you said in the meeting.
The thing you saw and did not stop.
And they add the second half of it, which is about the leader's own belief.
If the leader thinks the team cannot win, the team will not win, and the leader will not even notice they caused it, because the failure will confirm the belief.
The business version is a company with eight divisions, one of which consistently underperformed.
The chief executive was on the verge of firing the whole team.
The intervention was to fix the leader and the standards first, and the same people started producing.
Chapter three is Believe.
Willink's argument is that a leader cannot get a team to execute something they do not themselves believe in.

People read conviction with extraordinary accuracy, and a leader delivering a directive they privately think is stupid will telegraph it in every sentence, and the team will absorb the scepticism rather than the instruction.
The combat story is about a policy that the SEALs genuinely hated.
They were ordered to conduct operations partnered with Iraqi soldiers, jundis, who were often poorly trained, sometimes unreliable, occasionally a genuine danger, and who slowed everything down.
To highly trained special operators, this was not just annoying, it felt reckless.
Willink hated it too.
So he did the thing the chapter is actually about.
He went up the chain and asked why.
He kept asking until he understood.

And the answer, when it came, was strategically unarguable: the American forces were going to leave Iraq at some point, and if the Iraqi Army could not operate on its own, everything achieved at enormous cost would collapse the moment they left.
Building Iraqi capability was not a distraction from the mission.
It was the mission.
The operations his men were running were, in the long run, less important than the Iraqi soldiers learning to run them.
Once Willink understood that, he could believe it, and once he believed it, he could sell it.
And note what he did not do.
He did not go back and tell his men that headquarters had ordered it and there was nothing he could do.
That sentence, which is said every day in every organisation, is a leader publicly declaring that he is a bystander in his own command.
The rule they draw out: if you do not understand a directive, it is your responsibility to ask up the chain until you do.
Not to comply sullenly, and not to protect your subordinates from the decision by distancing yourself from it.
Ask why, understand the why, and then own it as though you had thought of it yourself.

The business case is a company rolling out a new compensation and profit distribution plan that its middle managers thought was unfair, and who therefore delivered it apologetically, which guaranteed the workforce would reject it.
Once those managers were walked through the actual economics of why the plan existed, they could deliver it with belief, and the resistance evaporated.
Chapter four is Check the Ego, and it is short and blunt.
Ego, they argue, is the single most common cause of failure they see in the field and in business.

It stops leaders admitting mistakes, prevents them accepting a better idea from a subordinate, makes them protect their own turf against the interests of the mission, and stops them planning honestly because honest planning requires acknowledging the ways you might be wrong.

The military example concerns a leader whose confidence in his own judgement stopped him from properly coordinating with adjacent units, on the grounds that his people were the elite and did not need to be slowed down by anyone else's process.
The resulting confusion put lives at risk.

The corporate example is an oil drilling company where a senior man on a rig blocked a new operating procedure, not because it was wrong, but because it had come from below him and adopting it felt like a concession.
Once his manager framed it so that adopting it was an act of leadership rather than an admission of defeat, the resistance disappeared overnight.
Willink's practical guidance here is genuinely useful.
Ego is not something to eliminate.
Ambition, drive and confidence come from the same place, and a leader with no ego at all is a leader with no fire.

The task is to keep it subordinate to the mission, and the way you check whether you have is to ask a specific question in any disagreement: am I resisting this because it is bad for the mission, or because it is bad for me?

There is a version of the ownership principle from Leif Babin's side of the story that I find even more instructive than Jocko's, because it is smaller and more ordinary, and most of us will never have a blue on blue incident but we will all have this.
Babin describes preparing his platoon for a mission and getting something wrong in the preparation.
Not spectacularly.
Just the sort of thing that happens: a detail that was not confirmed, an assumption carried forward, a piece of coordination that he believed had been handled and had not been.
And when it surfaced, his instinct, the instinct of every competent person in that situation, was to explain.
To point out the four reasons it was reasonable to have believed what he believed.

What he learned from watching Willink was that the explanation, however true, is corrosive, because it teaches everyone who hears it that in this outfit the correct response to a failure is a well constructed account of why it was not really your fault.
And once a team learns that, you can no longer find out what is actually going wrong, because every report you get has been pre-processed into a defence.
The alternative is almost absurdly simple and quite hard to do.
You say: that was mine, here is what I got wrong, here is what I am changing so it cannot happen again.
Then you stop talking.
No qualifiers, no context, no "although in fairness".
Babin's observation is that the first time a leader does this in front of their team, the room goes quiet, because people are waiting for the excuse and it does not come.

And within a few weeks other people start doing it, and the quality of information moving around the organisation improves dramatically, because reporting a problem has stopped being an admission of guilt and has become just a thing you do.
Now section two, which is the operational core of the book: the four Laws of Combat.
Law one, Cover and Move.
In its literal military form, this is the most basic tactic there is.
One element covers by firing at the enemy, which suppresses them, while another element moves.
Then they swap.
Nobody moves without someone covering.
It is how you cross open ground alive.
The organisational translation is teamwork, but with a specific edge to it.
Willink and Babin are not making a fluffy point about everyone getting along.
They are describing what happens when a large organisation splits into subgroups that begin to see each other, rather than the competition, as the enemy.
Their business case is a company where the field teams and the head office accounting group had gone to war.
The field people thought head office existed to obstruct them with paperwork.
The accountants thought the field people were cowboys who ignored the rules.
Both were partially right and both had entirely lost sight of the fact that they had the same customer and the same enemy.
The fix was to make each side responsible for the other's success rather than for their own defence.

The field leaders were sent to spend time understanding what the accounting group actually needed and why, and the accounting group was made to understand the operational cost of what they were asking for.
And the leadership principle underneath it: if a department you depend on is failing, that is not their problem which you are entitled to complain about.
It is your problem, because their failure will become your failure.
Willink's practical version: your job is not to protect your team from the other departments.
Your job is to help the other departments, because you cannot win alone.
Law two, Simple.
Plans must be simple, clear and concise.
Not because the people executing them are stupid, but because everything degrades under pressure.
Communications fail, people get hurt, half the information turns out to be wrong, and the plan has to survive being executed by exhausted people in the dark with partial information.
The test they use is excellent.
It is not whether the plan is clear to you.
It is whether it is clear to the most junior person who has to execute it, and the only way to know is to ask them to explain it back to you in their own words.
If they cannot, the plan is not simple, and it does not matter how elegant it looked in the briefing room.
Their business example is a factory where management introduced a bonus scheme intended to raise productivity, built on a complex formula with multiple weighted variables.
It failed completely, not because the workers did not want the money, but because none of them could work out what they personally needed to do differently to earn it.
An incentive nobody can compute is not an incentive.
When it was replaced with something a person on the line could understand in one sentence, output rose.
Law three, Prioritise and Execute.
This is the discipline for the moment when everything goes wrong at once, and Willink's shorthand for it is a phrase that has become well known: relax, look around, make a call.

The combat version is a compound where his men were, simultaneously, taking fire from more than one direction, dealing with a casualty, holding detainees, running low on ammunition, and needing to move before the situation got worse.
Every one of those problems was urgent and each demanded the commander's attention.
And a leader who tries to solve all of them at once solves none of them, and a leader who freezes because they cannot decide which one matters most is functionally absent.

So the drill is: take a breath, physically detach for a moment from the immediate chaos, assess the highest priority threat, state it out loud clearly so everyone knows what the priority is, direct the team's effort at that one thing, and then, and this is the part people miss, move to the next priority as soon as it is handled, and keep repeating.
Two refinements make it practical.
First, do not let the highest priority consume your entire focus, because while you are solving it another problem is developing behind you.
Maintain what they call situational awareness.
Second, plan ahead in quiet moments for what the likely priorities will be, so that when things break you are recognising a situation rather than meeting one.
And there is a physical skill inside this that Willink talks about more than almost anything else, which he calls detachment.

In the middle of a firefight, the natural thing for a leader to do is to become a shooter: to look through the sights at the immediate threat in front of them, because that is the most urgent, most vivid, most human thing to do.
And a leader who does that has just become one more rifle and stopped being a commander, at exactly the moment the team most needs someone with the whole picture.
So he trained himself, and trained his junior leaders, to physically take a step back.
To lower the weapon, to lift their eyes off the immediate problem, to turn around and look at what is happening behind and beside them.
He describes it as feeling deeply wrong every single time, and being the single most valuable thing he ever learned to do.
The office version is exact.

When the crisis lands, the pull is to dive into the spreadsheet, or get on the phone to the angry customer, or start rewriting the deck yourself, because that is concrete and satisfying and feels like leadership.
It is the opposite of leadership.
The move is to stand up, walk away from the screen for sixty seconds, and ask what the actual highest priority is, and whether the thing everyone is frantically working on is even in the top three.
Willink is also clear that the priority has to be spoken, loudly, and to everybody.
A leader who has silently decided what matters most has done half a job, because the team is still distributing its effort across all the problems.
Announce the priority, announce when it changes, and make sure the announcement travels down every level.

And the failure mode to watch for is the opposite of panic: it is a team quietly working very hard on the second, third and fourth most important things, because those are the tractable ones and the first one is frightening.
The business version is a startup chief executive with, at any given moment, eleven top priorities.
Which means no priorities.
The intervention is simply forcing a ranking, in order, and getting the whole organisation aimed at the first one until it is done.
Law four, Decentralised Command.
This is, I think, the most valuable chapter in the book for anyone running an organisation of any size.
The observation is that human beings can effectively lead somewhere between four and six people directly.
Beyond that, direct control breaks down.
So SEAL units are built in small teams with a leader at every level, and every one of those junior leaders is expected to make decisions on their own.
But that only works if two conditions hold.

The junior leader must understand not only what to do but why, meaning the overall intent and the desired end state, so that when the plan fails they can improvise something that still serves the goal.
And they must know exactly the boundaries of their authority: what they can decide alone, and what genuinely requires escalation.

Willink's illustration of what happens without it is a training exercise where a very capable commander tried to run everything himself, taking every radio call and making every decision, and the whole operation ground to a halt while a queue of subordinates waited for permission to do things they were perfectly capable of deciding.
And the flip side, which he is equally firm about: decentralised command is not the absence of leadership.
A leader who tells his people to use their judgement and then disappears has not decentralised anything, he has abdicated.

Senior leaders must stay close enough to know what is going on, must physically position themselves where they can see the whole picture rather than getting sucked into one part of the fight, and must resist both extremes: micromanaging on one side, and vanishing on the other.

The business application is the one every growing company hits: the founder who was the decision maker at fifteen people and is now the bottleneck at a hundred and fifty, and whose organisation has quietly learned that nothing can be decided without them.
Section three is Sustaining Victory, and it is about the systems that keep the first eight principles alive.
Chapter nine is Plan.
They lay out an actual planning process, and its most interesting features are the counterintuitive ones.
First, the mission must be clear and simple, and it must be expressed in terms of the end state you want, not the tasks to be performed.
A team that knows the intent can adapt.
A team that only knows the task list is helpless the moment reality departs from the list.
Second, and this is the one most organisations get wrong: the senior leader should not write the plan.
Delegate the planning to the junior leaders closest to the work.
Two reasons.
They know details you do not, and, more importantly, people execute a plan they helped build with a completely different level of ownership than a plan handed down to them.
Third, the senior leader's job during planning is not to invent the plan but to stand back and check it.
To ask what happens if this fails, and this, and this.
To hunt for the assumptions nobody has questioned.
And to keep asking whether it can be made simpler.
Fourth, brief it, then test the brief.
Ask the most junior people to explain their part.
If they cannot, you have not briefed, you have talked.
They also give the actual sequence a SEAL planning cycle runs through, and it is worth having, because it is a checklist you can lift straight into a project meeting.
Analyse the mission and restate it in your own words, including the commander's intent one level above you, so you know what your boss's boss is trying to achieve.
Identify the resources you actually have, personnel, time, money, and the ones you could ask for.
Decompose the mission into achievable phases.

Develop a specific course of action, and then, importantly, develop contingencies for the most likely points of failure, not for every conceivable disaster, which is how planning turns into paralysis.
Assign responsibility by name to each phase, so that nothing is owned by "the team".
Then brief it, confirm understanding, and execute.
The contingency discipline is the part most organisations skip.
Willink's version of the question is not "what could go wrong", which produces a useless list of a hundred items.
It is "what are the three most likely ways this fails, and what do we do in each case", which produces something you can actually brief in ninety seconds.
And fifth, debrief afterwards, every time, win or lose.
What went right, what went wrong, what do we change.

Willink is insistent that this is where almost all improvement actually comes from, and that the debrief must be brutally honest and must not become a search for someone to punish, because the moment it does, people stop reporting what really happened and you are blind.
Chapter ten is Leading Up and Down the Chain of Command, and it contains the most useful reframe in the book for anyone with a difficult boss.
Willink describes his own frustration with higher headquarters.
They kept asking for more information, more paperwork, more justification before approving his operations.
From where he sat, this was bureaucrats slowing down a war.
Then he had the realisation that turned it around.
If his boss did not have enough information to be comfortable approving an operation, whose fault was that?
His.
He had not been sending enough information up.
He had been treating the chain of command as an obstacle rather than as a team that needed something from him.
So he started sending far more detail than was requested, proactively, before being asked.
The requests for paperwork stopped, and approvals came faster.
The principle: if your leadership is not giving you what you need, the most likely cause is that you have not communicated well enough.
And the harder version, which they state plainly: it is not your boss's job to work out what you need.
It is your job to make them understand.
Leading down the chain is the mirror image.
Your people need to know why, not just what.
When a team does not understand the reason for something, they invent one, and the invented reason is almost always more cynical than the truth.
Chapter eleven is Decisiveness Amid Uncertainty.
The claim: there is no such thing as one hundred percent certainty, and there never will be.
Waiting for complete information is itself a decision, and usually the worst one available.
The combat illustration is a moment where a vehicle came fast toward a position, in circumstances that were genuinely ambiguous.
There was no time to gather more information, and both possible errors were catastrophic in opposite directions.
Willink's point is not that he made the correct call by superior insight.
It is that he made a call, quickly, on the best information available, and was prepared to adjust immediately if new information arrived.

The habits that make this possible: know your standard operating procedures cold, so that most situations resolve into a known pattern; think through likely scenarios in advance so that decision time is recognition time; be decisive but not stubborn, willing to reverse instantly when the picture changes; and understand that a decent decision made now generally beats a perfect decision made too late.
Chapter twelve is Discipline Equals Freedom, and it is the philosophical close.
Willink's own version is famous and slightly absurd: he wakes at four thirty in the morning, every day, and for years posted a photograph of his watch at that hour.
The point of the ritual is not the hour.
It is that discipline in the small, non negotiable things builds the capacity for discipline in the large ones.
The paradox in the title is genuine.
Rigid standard operating procedures, drilled until they are automatic, do not restrict a team.
They liberate it, because when the procedures are automatic, the team's conscious attention is freed for the things that are actually novel.
A team with no standard procedures must think about everything, and therefore thinks about nothing well.
Financial discipline produces the freedom to make choices.
Physical discipline produces the freedom of a body that can do what you ask of it.

And then, in the final pages, they introduce the idea that they later expanded into a whole second book, and which is, in my view, the most sophisticated thing in this one: the Dichotomy of Leadership.
Every leadership principle in this book, they say, is dangerous taken to its extreme.
So a leader must live in the tension between opposites.
A leader must be confident, but never cocky.
Brave, but not reckless.
Competitive, but a gracious loser.
Attentive to detail, but not obsessed by detail to the point of losing the big picture.
Strong, but with endurance.
A leader, and also a follower, able to take direction from someone else.
Humble, but not passive.
Aggressive, but not overbearing.
Quiet, but not silent.
Calm, but not robotic, still capable of showing real emotion when it matters.
Close to the team, but never so close to any one person that they become more important than the team's welfare or the mission itself.
Willing to hold people accountable, but not to hold their hand.
That list is the honest correction to everything else in the book.
Extreme Ownership taken to an extreme becomes a leader who takes on everything personally and micromanages every task.
Decentralised Command taken to an extreme becomes abdication.
Simple taken to an extreme becomes simplistic.
The skill is not in picking a side.
It is in knowing which way you personally lean and correcting for it.
Now let me be a fair guide and give you the honest caveats.
The military framing is a genuine strength and a genuine limitation.
Combat produces a clarity that business rarely has: an unambiguous enemy, an obvious mission, and lives at stake, which makes people accept authority in a way employees do not.
Some of the transfers land perfectly.
Some feel a little forced, and the business case studies are written by consultants about their own clients, so they always end in success, which is not how consulting actually goes.

There is also a real critique of Extreme Ownership as a doctrine, which is worth naming: pushed too hard it can become a tool for absorbing blame that genuinely belongs elsewhere, including with senior leadership, or a way of telling people that structural problems are personal failures.
Willink's own answer is the Dichotomy chapter, and, to be fair, his version of ownership runs upward as hard as it runs downward.
But you should hold it as a leadership stance rather than as a description of how causation actually works.
And I want to say something about the human weight underneath this book, because it is easy to read it as a set of business tips and miss what it cost.
Task Unit Bruiser lost men in Ramadi.
Marc Lee was killed in a firefight in August 2006, the first SEAL to die in Iraq.
On the same day, Ryan Job was hit in the face by a sniper's round and permanently blinded, and died a few years later from complications following surgery.
In September, Michael Monsoor threw himself onto a grenade that landed among his teammates on a rooftop, absorbing the blast with his own body and saving the men beside him.
He was awarded the Medal of Honor.
Willink and Babin dedicate the book to them, and the reason that matters for the reader is this: the ownership principle in chapter one is not a rhetorical device for these two men.
When they say a leader is responsible for everything that happens under his command, they are also saying it about the days their friends did not come home.
That is what makes the book's tone what it is, and it is why the sternness in it never reads as posturing.
So let me leave you with what to actually do.
First, on the next thing that goes wrong, run the Extreme Ownership hypothesis before you run any other explanation.
Assume, as an exercise, that it is entirely your fault, and write down what you would have had to do differently.
You will nearly always find two or three real actions, where the blaming version gives you none.
Second, look at what you are tolerating.
Walk your operation and note every substandard thing you have walked past without comment in the last month.
Each one is now your published standard.
Pick the two worst and address them this week.
Third, when you are given a directive you do not believe in, go and ask why until you understand it, and then own it in your own voice.
Never deliver something to your team with the words, they are making us do this.
Fourth, in any disagreement, ask yourself the ego question: am I resisting this because it is bad for the mission, or because it is bad for me?
Say the honest answer out loud, at least to yourself.
Fifth, test your plans for simplicity by asking the most junior person involved to explain their part back to you.
Not "does that make sense", which always gets a yes.
Ask them to say it.
Sixth, when everything breaks at once, do the drill: detach for ten seconds, identify the single highest priority, say it out loud so everyone hears it, direct effort at that, then move to the next.

Seventh, if you have more than about six people reporting to you, build leaders underneath you and give them two things in writing: the intent and end state, so they can improvise, and the limits of their decision authority, so they know when to escalate.
Eighth, if your boss is frustrating you, assume first that you have under communicated.
Send more information than is asked for, before it is asked for, and watch how much of the friction disappears.
And ninth, debrief everything.
Wins as well as losses.
What went right, what went wrong, what changes.
Do it fast, do it honestly, and never let it become a hunt for someone to punish, because the day it does is the day people start telling you what you want to hear.
The single sentence to carry out of this book is the one Jocko said in that room in Ramadi when he had every excuse available to him and a list of true ones in his hand.
There is only one person to blame for this.
Me.
Not because it was literally, mechanically true in every particular.
But because it was the only place to stand from which anything could be fixed.
